Introduction to Dietary Intake Patterns

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey was conducted by the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention. This survey collects a vast amount of dietary data from 2 seperate and thousands of people. In this data analysis we took data from August 2021 to August 2023. This data was used to draw conclusions on the health of the participants in the survey.

## combibing of datasets
diet<-dr1|>select(SEQN, DR1TKCAL, DR1TPROT, DR1TSODI, DR1TTFAT,DR1TCAFF, DR1_320Z)|>inner_join(dr2|>select(SEQN, DR2TKCAL, DR2TPROT,DR2TCAFF, DR2_320Z), by="SEQN")
## Average Caffeine dataset
caffeine<-diet|>mutate(avg_caffeine=(DR1TCAFF+DR2TCAFF)/2)|>na.omit()

Histogram regarding Caffeine Intake

Caffeine is considered a necessity for the majority of Americans. Most Americans start their day brewing coffee, stopping at their local coffee shop, or injesting their caffeine via other ways such as energy drinks or pills.

## Distribution of Average Daily Caffeine intake
ggplot(caffeine, aes(x = avg_caffeine)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=10, fill="aquamarine3", color="white")+
  labs(title = "Distribution of Average Daily Caffeine Intake",
    x ="Average Caffeine Intake (mg)",
    y ="Number of Participants")+
  xlim(0,1000)+
  ylim(0,500)
## Warning: Removed 14 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_bin()`).
## Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_bar()`).

The mean caffeine intake was 115.5 mg and the standard deviation was 146.8 mg.

Looking at the graph we see an obvious skew right, more on that later. We see that a large portion of participants don’t drink any caffeine at all and the average person drinks about 115 milligrams of caffeine, which is about 2-3 cups of coffee, this is unsurprising to me. However an issue arises in this data set, the skewness of the graph shows people drinking well over 400 miligrams of caffeine per day. This is red flag because according to the Food and Drug Administration, 400 milligrams is considered the safe limit. There is a large portion well over that limit. This leads me to believe there was an issue in reporting.

Scatterplot on how many calories were had over 2 days

## amount of calories had over 2 days
calories<-diet|>filter(!is.na(DR1TKCAL), !is.na(DR2TKCAL))

Calories are one of the most conversed about things when the American diet is mentioned. Americans are known for over consuming on calories leading to an abundance of health issues that significantly affects Americans day to day lives.

## Scatter plot comparing calories over the two days
ggplot(calories, aes(x=DR1TKCAL, y=DR2TKCAL))+
  geom_point(alpha = 1, color = "black") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE, color="red")+
  labs(title = "Caloric Intake: Day 1 vs Day 2",
    x ="Day 1 Calories (kcal)",
    y ="Day 2 Calories (kcal)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

This scatter plot is the amount of calories consumed over the 2 reported days. This does two things, first it tests if participants are consistent with their calories consumption, and two tests to see if the data is reliable. We see that there is a somewhat strong correlation so both tests check out. According to the National Health Service, 2000 to 2500 KCals is required per day, we see most fall in between that range.

Sodium Intake and Water Consumption

##Comparing Sodium and water, mutated water to it into 3 groups
## Summary statistic also included.
sodium_water<-diet|>
  filter(!is.na(DR1_320Z),!is.na(DR1TSODI))|>
  mutate(water_category=case_when(
    DR1_320Z<2700 ~ "Below Recommended (<2700 g)",
    DR1_320Z<3700 ~ "Within Recommended (2700–3700 g)",
    DR1_320Z>3700 ~ "Above Recommended (>3700 g)"))|>
  mutate(water_category=factor(
    water_category,
    levels = c("Below Recommended (<2700 g)","Within Recommended (2700–3700 g)",
    "Above Recommended (>3700 g)")))

sodium_summary <- sodium_water |>
  group_by(water_category) |>
  summarize(mean_sodium = mean(DR1TSODI, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_sodium = sd(DR1TSODI, na.rm = TRUE))

This next data analysis is on water consumption and sodium intake. Water is as important to humans as oxygen, without the correct amount of water humans can have serious health complications and even death. An important component of water consumption is the amount of sodium paired with it. Sodium consumption and water consumption need to be well balanced to have a healthy life.

### Boxplot of water consumption and Sodium Intake
ggplot(sodium_water, aes(x=water_category, y=DR1TSODI))+
  geom_boxplot(fill="steelblue")+
  labs(title="Sodium Intake by Water Intake Level",
    x="Daily Water Intake Category (grams)",
    y="Sodium Intake (mg)")

Participants below the recommended water intake had an average sodium consumption of 2908.3 mg.

According to the Mayo Clinic, 2,700-3,700 grams of water per day is optimal however that is combined with the assumption that sodium intake is under control. According to the American Heart Association, 1,500 mg of sodium per day is optimal. The boxplot supplies us with a few important pieces of information, first the average sodium intake (about ~2600 mg) is way too high in every group although it is technically healthier in the group that had an above recommended intake of water. But this is incredibly dangerous for the participants with below average water intake, as referenced above its at about 2908.3 mg. While a water increase in these participants wouldn’t hurt, what they need to focus on is lowering their sodium intake.

Conclusion

Analyzing data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey highlights several things within the American diet. Caffeine intake is considered normal with a few outliers, such far outliers that death is almost guaranteed, more probable is there was inaccurate reporting. This assumption can also be applied to sodium intake as more than 10,000 mg a day is considered very dangerous. We found that the participants were largely within the normal range of calories per day, however, there was still a large portion that was much higher than what is recommended. That paired with the sodium and water consumption shows us how unhealthy Americans are. Using this data we can conclude that most Americans need to rethink their diet and focus more on healthy options.
